lessons.title: Burning fuels
lessons.bigQuestion: Where does a candle go when it burns?
objectives: To understand combustion as a reaction between a fuel and oxygen that releases energy
successCriteria: All: name the reactants and products of burning a hydrocarbon
Most: write a word equation for complete combustion
Some: explain why mass seems to be lost when a fuel burns
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: fossil fuels and energy supply
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: fuels as Allah's provision stored in the earth

keywords.def: burning: a fuel reacting with oxygen
a substance that releases energy when burned
a compound of hydrogen and carbon only
a substance that reacts
a substance made in a reaction

hook.text: A candle gets shorter as it burns. Where has the wax gone?
hook.a: It reacts with oxygen and becomes carbon dioxide and water vapour, which escape into the air.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Have you seen the fire that you kindle? Is it you who produced its tree, or are We the Producer?' (al-Waqi'ah 56:71-72). Fire and fuels are gifts from Allah that we must use carefully.

starter.q: Name the gas in air we need to burn things.
Write the chemical formula of water.

teach.heading: Fuel + oxygen
bullets: Hydrocarbons make carbon dioxide and water

model.problem: Write a word equation for burning methane
steps: Reactants: methane + oxygen
Products of a hydrocarbon: carbon dioxide + water
methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water

teach.heading: Testing the products
bullets: Water: blue cobalt chloride paper turns pink (or anhydrous copper sulfate turns blue)
teach.note: Teacher demo video: candle under a funnel, gases drawn through a cooled tube and limewater.

teach.heading: Where does the mass go?
bullets: If we collected them, the mass would increase
teach.note: Answer the big question: oxygen from the air is added, so the products weigh more than the wax that burnt.

misconception.wrong: Burning destroys matter
misconception.right: Atoms are rearranged into gases; mass is conserved

check.q: A gas turns limewater milky. It is…
check.why: Limewater is the test for carbon dioxide. Water is tested with cobalt chloride or copper sulfate.

practice.q: Write the word equation for propane burning completely.
practice.model:
Reactants: the fuel (propane) and oxygen.
Products of any hydrocarbon burning completely: carbon dioxide and water.
So propane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.

practice.q: How do we test for water?
practice.a: Blue cobalt chloride paper turns pink (or white anhydrous copper sulfate turns blue).

practice.q: Is combustion exothermic or endothermic?

independent.q: Core: Write word equations for burning methane, butane and hydrogen.
independent.a: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; butane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; hydrogen + oxygen → water.
independent.model:
Teacher writes methane first: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
Hydrocarbon in, carbon dioxide and water out.

independent.q: Extend: Why does hydrogen make no carbon dioxide when it burns?
independent.a: It contains no carbon atoms.

independent.q: Stretch: A candle on a balance loses mass as it burns. Explain why this does not break the law of conservation of mass. Write in the portal response box.
independent.a: The products (carbon dioxide and water vapour) escape as gases; if collected, the total mass of products would equal the wax and oxygen used.

exit.q: The products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon are...
exit.a: Carbon dioxide and water

exit.q: Big question: where does a candle go when it burns?
exit.a: The wax reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water vapour, which escape into the air.

keywords.def: a reaction where a substance gains oxygen
a compound of an element with oxygen
mass is not created or destroyed in a reaction
slow oxidation of iron with water and oxygen
gives out energy

hook.text: Magnesium ribbon burns with a blinding white light and the ash weighs more than the ribbon. Where did the extra mass come from?
hook.a: From oxygen in the air, which joined the magnesium.

starter.q: Products of complete combustion of methane?

starter.a: A compound of hydrogen and carbon only.

teach.heading: Oxidation
teach.note: Show magnesium ribbon burning (video; bright light, do not look directly).

teach.heading: Mass increases
bullets: Magnesium oxide weighs more than magnesium

model.problem: 2.4 g of magnesium burns to make 4.0 g of magnesium oxide. What mass of oxygen reacted?

Oxygen = product − magnesium

teach.heading: Burning vs rusting
bullets: Rusting is slow and needs water too

misconception.wrong: Magnesium loses mass when it burns, like wood
misconception.right: It gains oxygen, so the solid product is heavier

check.q: What forms when copper is heated in air?
check.why: Copper + oxygen → copper oxide. Heating in air supplies oxygen.

practice.q: 3.6 g magnesium makes 6.0 g magnesium oxide. Mass of oxygen?
practice.model:
Mass is conserved.
Oxygen = product - metal.
6.0 - 3.6 = 2.4.

practice.q: Write the word equation for iron reacting with oxygen.
What two things does iron need to rust?

independent.q: Core: Write word equations for copper, zinc and calcium reacting with oxygen.
independent.a: copper + oxygen → copper oxide; zinc + oxygen → zinc oxide; calcium + oxygen → calcium oxide.
independent.model:

Metal + oxygen → metal oxide.

independent.q: Extend: 6.4 g copper gains 1.6 g oxygen. What mass of copper oxide forms?

independent.a: Wood's products are mostly gases that escape; magnesium oxide is a solid that keeps the oxygen it gained.

exit.q: Oxidation means...
exit.a: Gaining oxygen

exit.q: Big question: why does magnesium get heavier but wood lighter when burned?
exit.a: Magnesium gains oxygen into a solid oxide; wood's products are gases that escape.

lessons.title: Combustion products: the candle demonstration
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we prove what a candle makes when it burns?

keywords.def: a solution that turns milky with carbon dioxide
blue paper that turns pink with water
water vapour cooling into droplets
what we see, hear or measure
a conclusion drawn from observations

hook.text: A glass held above a candle mists up. A jar placed over a candle puts it out. What two clues do these give?
hook.a: The mist shows water is a product; the flame going out shows oxygen is used up.

starter.a: Cobalt chloride paper turns blue to pink

teach.heading: Teacher demonstration
bullets: Then a jar over the candle
teach.note: Teacher only, on camera. Pupils do not light candles for this lesson.

teach.heading: Observations
bullets: Flame goes out under the jar
teach.note: Separate what we see from what we conclude.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: The flame does not 'use up all the air'

misconception.wrong: The candle uses up all the air
misconception.right: It uses some of the oxygen (about 21% of air); most of the air is nitrogen, which does not burn

check.q: The cold glass above the candle mists up. This shows...
check.why: Water vapour from combustion condenses on the cold glass.

practice.q: Doubling the jar volume roughly... the burning time.
practice.a: Doubles (8 s to 17 s to 35 s).
practice.model:
Compare: 250 to 500 cm³ is double; time goes 8 to 17 s, about double.
500 to 1000, time 17 to 35, about double.
So time is roughly proportional to volume: more oxygen, longer burn.

practice.q: Is 'the glass misted' an observation or an inference?
Why does the flame go out?
practice.a: Too little oxygen is left to keep it burning.

independent.q: Core: Write up the demonstration: equipment, observations, inferences and the word equation for paraffin wax burning.
independent.a: Observations and inferences as above; wax + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
independent.model:
Teacher writes the first line: 'Observation: a cold glass held above the flame misted up.
Inference: water is a product.'

independent.q: Extend: Predict the time for a 750 cm³ jar and explain.
independent.a: About 26 s: between 17 and 35 s, as time is roughly proportional to volume (oxygen available).

independent.q: Stretch: Suggest why repeating the test gives slightly different times.
independent.a: Draughts, wick length, how quickly the jar was placed, candle size.

exit.q: Limewater turns milky with...
exit.a: Carbon dioxide

exit.q: Big question: how can we prove what a candle makes when it burns?
exit.a: Test the products: water mists a cold glass (or turns cobalt chloride pink) and carbon dioxide turns limewater milky.

check.q: A TV catches fire. What is safest?
options: Turn off the power at the wall if safe, use a CO₂ extinguisher, get out and call 999
check.why: Water conducts electricity. Cutting power removes heat source; CO₂ removes oxygen. Safety first: get out and call 999.

practice.q: A fire blanket is put over a pan fire. Which side of the triangle is removed?
practice.model:
What does the blanket do?
Covers the fire.
What can no longer reach the flame?
Air, so oxygen.
So the oxygen side is removed and the fire goes out.

practice.q: Which side does water remove?
Why must you not use water on an electrical fire?
practice.a: Water conducts electricity, so you could be electrocuted.

independent.q: Core: For five fires (bin, pan of oil, TV, forest, gas cooker), say the best way to put it out and which side is removed.
independent.a: Bin: water (heat); pan of oil: fire blanket, turn off heat (oxygen, heat); TV: power off, CO₂ extinguisher (oxygen); forest: firebreak (fuel); gas cooker: turn off gas (fuel).
independent.model: Teacher does the bin first: paper fire, use water, removes heat.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why a chip-pan fire becomes a fireball when water is added. Write in the portal response box.
independent.a: Water sinks below the hot oil, boils instantly to steam, which expands and throws burning oil droplets into the air.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain the rule 'get out, stay out, call 999' using what smoke contains.
independent.a: Smoke contains carbon monoxide and hot toxic gases that can kill in minutes, so escape is safer than fighting the fire.

exit.q: Which is NOT a side of the fire triangle?
exit.a: Water

exit.q: Big question: how does a fire blanket put out a pan fire?
exit.a: It cuts off the oxygen supply, removing one side of the fire triangle.

practice.q: Write a word equation for methane burning with very little oxygen.

practice.model:
Limited oxygen means the carbon cannot become carbon dioxide.
It becomes carbon monoxide (or carbon).
Hydrogen still becomes water.

practice.q: What colour flame shows incomplete combustion?

independent.q: Stretch: Why are CO alarms recommended near gas boilers?

exit.q: Which gas is made only in incomplete combustion?

exit.q: Big question: why is a yellow, smoky flame more dangerous than a blue one?
exit.a: It shows incomplete combustion, which makes poisonous carbon monoxide and soot.

hook.a: Natural levels keep Earth habitable; extra gases from human activity trap too much heat.

cycle: Earth warms and gives off heat

practice.q: Describe the greenhouse effect in four steps.
practice.a: Sunlight warms the Earth; Earth gives off heat (infrared); greenhouse gases absorb some; they re-radiate it, keeping Earth warm.
practice.model: Step 1: sunlight reaches and warms the Earth. Step 2: the Earth gives off heat. Step 3: greenhouse gases absorb some of it. Step 4: they send some back down, so the Earth stays warmer.

practice.q: By how much did CO₂ rise from 1800 to 2024 (table)?

independent.q: Core: Write a paragraph explaining how burning fossil fuels contributes to global warming (portal response box). Start: 'When fossil fuels burn...'
independent.a: When fossil fuels burn they release carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas; more CO₂ absorbs and re-radiates more heat, so average temperatures rise.
independent.model: Teacher writes the model: Point: burning fossil fuels releases CO₂. Explain: CO₂ absorbs heat given off by Earth. Link: more CO₂ means more heat trapped, so global temperatures rise.

independent.q: Extend: Give two consequences of global warming.
independent.a: Rising sea levels, more extreme weather, melting ice, changes to habitats and crops.

independent.q: Stretch: 'CO₂ and temperature both rose, so one caused the other.' Is this good reasoning? Explain.
independent.a: Correlation alone does not prove cause; scientists also understand the mechanism and test it, which is why they are confident.

exit.q: Which is a greenhouse gas?
exit.a: Methane

exit.q: Big question: if the greenhouse effect keeps us alive, why is it a problem?
exit.a: Extra greenhouse gases from human activity trap more heat, so the Earth warms beyond its natural balance.

lessons.bigQuestion: Why do climbers on very high mountains get tired so quickly, even when they rest?
objectives: To understand how red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to respiring cells
successCriteria: All: describe the job of haemoglobin
Most: explain two adaptations of red blood cells
Some: explain how carbon monoxide reduces oxygen transport
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: home safety and CO alarms
lessons.smsc: Moral: protecting family from hidden dangers

keywords.def: the red protein that carries oxygen
a cell that carries oxygen
the liquid part of blood
haemoglobin joined to oxygen
a poisonous gas that blocks haemoglobin

hook.text: Why do climbers on very high mountains get tired so quickly, even when they rest?
hook.a: There is less oxygen in each breath, so less reaches the cells for respiration.

starter.q: Which side of the heart pumps to the body?

teach.heading: Haemoglobin
bullets: Joins with oxygen in the lungs

teach.heading: Red cell adaptations
bullets: No nucleus: more room for haemoglobin
Small and flexible: squeeze through capillaries

teach.heading: Carbon monoxide
bullets: From faulty boilers, car exhaust, cigarettes
Binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen
teach.note: CO alarms save lives at home.

check.q: Why does a red blood cell have no nucleus?
check.why: More haemoglobin means more oxygen carried.

practice.q: Explain why carbon monoxide is dangerous.
practice.a: It joins haemoglobin instead of oxygen, so less oxygen reaches cells for respiration
practice.model: What carries oxygen? Haemoglobin. What does CO do? Takes its place. So less oxygen gets to cells, and respiration slows.

practice.q: Name the part of blood that carries glucose.
Give one adaptation of red blood cells.
practice.a: No nucleus, biconcave shape, or small and flexible

independent.q: Core: Draw a red blood cell (top and side view) and label three adaptations with their benefit.
independent.a: Biconcave disc (surface area), no nucleus (more haemoglobin), small and flexible (fits capillaries)
independent.model: Teacher draws the side view on screen: a disc thinner in the middle.

independent.q: Extend: Why do people who live at high altitude often have more red blood cells?
independent.a: To carry enough oxygen when each breath has less oxygen.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why a CO alarm is needed near a gas boiler.
independent.a: Faulty burning makes CO, which has no smell or colour; an alarm detects it before people are harmed.

exit.q: Haemoglobin carries...
exit.a: Oxygen

exit.q: Big question: why do climbers tire quickly high up?
exit.a: Less oxygen per breath reaches their cells for respiration.

lessons.homework: Check with an adult whether your home has a carbon monoxide alarm and where it is. Write why it is there.
lessons.send: SEND: labelled diagram to copy. EAL: haemoglobin, oxygen, carry. Stretch: research sickle cell anaemia's effect on oxygen transport.

lessons.title: Gas exchange in other organisms
lessons.bigQuestion: A fish drowns in air and you drown in water. Why can't each use the other's oxygen?
objectives: To understand how fish, insects and plants exchange gases in different ways
successCriteria: All: describe how fish gills work
Most: describe spiracles and tracheae in insects
Some: explain how stomata let leaves exchange gases
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: oxygen in rivers and fish health
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the variety of ways living things breathe

keywords.def: organs that take oxygen from water
a small hole in an insect's body for air
tubes carrying air inside an insect
tiny pores in a leaf
cells that open and close stomata

hook.text: A fish drowns in air and you drown in water. Why can't each use the other's oxygen?
hook.a: Gills collapse in air and stick together; lungs cannot extract dissolved oxygen from water.

teach.heading: Fish: gills
bullets: Water in through the mouth, out over gills
teach.note: Water flows one way; oxygen diffuses into the blood.

teach.heading: Insects: spiracles and tracheae
bullets: Tubes take air straight to cells

teach.heading: Plants: stomata
bullets: Pores mostly on the underside of leaves
CO₂ in for photosynthesis, O₂ out
Guard cells open and close them

teach.heading: Compare
teach.note: Common features: large surface area, thin, moist.

check.q: What do all gas exchange surfaces share?
options: Large surface area and thin surface
check.why: Large and thin surfaces make diffusion fast.

practice.q: Why are gill filaments thin and many?
practice.a: Large surface area and short distance for oxygen to diffuse into the blood
practice.model: Many filaments: large surface. Thin: short distance. Both speed diffusion of oxygen into the blood.

practice.q: Where are most stomata?
How does air reach an insect's cells?

independent.q: Core: Look at the underside of a leaf with a magnifying glass (or the class micrograph). Draw what you see and label stomata and guard cells from the micrograph.
independent.a: Drawing of leaf surface; stomata as pores between two guard cells
independent.model: Teacher shows the leaf micrograph on screen and labels one stoma.

independent.q: Extend: Write a comparison paragraph in the portal response box: human lungs and fish gills. Starter: 'Both lungs and gills...'
independent.a: Both have a large surface area, thin surfaces and a rich blood supply; lungs take oxygen from air, gills from water.

independent.q: Stretch: Why can't insects grow as large as a cat?
independent.a: Air must diffuse along the tracheae; tubes become too long for enough oxygen to reach the cells.

exit.q: Leaves exchange gases through...
exit.a: Stomata

exit.q: Big question: why can't a fish breathe in air?
exit.a: Gills collapse and stick together in air, so the surface area falls.

lessons.homework: Paint clear nail varnish on the underside of a leaf with an adult, peel it with tape and look at the stomata print with a magnifying glass.
lessons.send: SEND: labelled micrograph. EAL: gills, stomata. Stretch: research counter-current flow in gills.

lessons.title: Smoking and the gas exchange system
lessons.bigQuestion: If smoking is so harmful, why do people start, and why is it so hard to stop?
objectives: To understand how smoking damages the gas exchange system and the rest of the body
successCriteria: All: name the harmful substances in cigarette smoke
Most: explain how tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide cause harm
Some: use data to describe the link between smoking and lung cancer
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: drugs, choices and health
lessons.smsc: Moral: protecting the body Allah entrusted to us

keywords.def: a sticky substance in smoke that coats the lungs and can cause cancer
an addictive drug in tobacco
tiny hairs that sweep mucus out of airways
hard to stop using
a substance that can cause cancer

hook.text: If smoking is so harmful, why do people start, and why is it so hard to stop?
hook.a: Peer pressure, advertising and curiosity; nicotine is addictive.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction' (Al-Baqarah 2:195), and 'do not kill yourselves' (An-Nisa 4:29). Many scholars rule smoking forbidden because of the harm it does to the smoker and to others.

teach.heading: The damage
bullets: Smoke paralyses cilia: mucus builds up, 'smoker's cough'

teach.heading: The evidence
bullets: Smokers are far more likely to get lung cancer
teach.note: Approximate, from UK cancer statistics: about 7 in 10 lung cancer cases in the UK are caused by smoking.

teach.heading: Choosing well
bullets: Say no to smoking and vaping
teach.note: Vapes contain nicotine too and are illegal to sell to under-18s in the UK.

check.q: Why do smokers often cough?
options: Cilia are damaged so mucus builds up
check.why: Paralysed cilia cannot sweep mucus away, so the body coughs it up.

practice.q: Explain why smokers get breathless.
practice.a: Tar and damage reduce alveoli surface area, and CO lowers oxygen carried, so less oxygen reaches cells
practice.model: Two effects. Lungs: tar and damaged alveoli mean less surface for diffusion. Blood: CO takes haemoglobin's place. Both mean less oxygen to cells.

practice.q: What makes cigarettes addictive?
Name a carcinogen in smoke.

independent.q: Core: Write a letter in the portal response box persuading an adult relative to stop smoking, using three scientific facts and kindness. Starter: 'I care about you, and I learnt that...'
independent.a: Pupils' own; facts such as tar causes cancer, CO reduces oxygen, about 7 in 10 lung cancers are caused by smoking; respectful tone
independent.model: Teacher writes the opening on screen: 'I care about you, and in science I learnt that tar in smoke coats the lungs.'

independent.q: Extend: Why is second-hand smoke harmful to children in the home?
independent.a: They breathe in the same tar, CO and carcinogens; their lungs are still developing.

independent.q: Stretch: Why might the link between smoking and cancer take years to show?
independent.a: Cancers develop slowly after years of damage; long studies were needed.

exit.q: Tar in smoke...
exit.a: Coats the lungs and can cause cancer
options: Coats the lungs and can cause cancer

exit.q: Big question: why is it hard to stop smoking?
exit.a: Nicotine is addictive.

lessons.homework: Find the NHS Smokefree help line or website with an adult and write one way it helps people quit.
lessons.send: SEND: letter frame with fact bank. EAL: harm, addict, damage. Stretch: compare smoking and vaping evidence.

lessons.title: Anaerobic respiration in humans
lessons.bigQuestion: After a 100 m sprint you keep panting for minutes, even though you have stopped. Why?
objectives: To understand how muscles release energy without oxygen and why this causes an oxygen debt
successCriteria: All: write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in muscles
Most: compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration
Some: explain why we keep panting after exercise
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: line graphs over time
lessons.smsc: Moral: looking after health with sensible exercise

keywords.def: without oxygen
the product of anaerobic respiration in muscles
extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid
tiredness of muscles
a short, very fast run

hook.text: After a 100 m sprint you keep panting for minutes, even though you have stopped. Why?
hook.a: Muscles respired anaerobically, making lactic acid; extra oxygen is needed to break it down (oxygen debt).

teach.heading: When oxygen runs short
bullets: Hard exercise: not enough oxygen delivered

teach.heading: Oxygen debt
bullets: Lactic acid builds up: fatigue, cramp

teach.heading: Example data
bullets: Breathing rate during and after a sprint

check.q: Anaerobic respiration in muscles produces...
check.why: glucose → lactic acid in human muscles.

practice.q: Use the chart: how long did breathing take to return to near rest?
practice.model: Rest is 14. Read along: 6 minutes after, it is 15, almost back. So about 6 minutes.

practice.q: Why do muscles get tired in a sprint?
Which releases more energy per glucose: aerobic or anaerobic?

independent.q: Core: Count your breaths for 1 minute at rest, then after 1 minute of gentle stepping on the bottom stair, then every minute for 4 minutes. Record and plot a line graph.
independent.a: Pupils' own; rate rises then falls back towards rest
independent.model: Teacher counts own resting breaths on camera: '15 per minute.'

independent.q: Extend: Explain your graph using 'oxygen debt'.
independent.a: Breathing stayed high after stepping to supply extra oxygen to break down lactic acid.

independent.q: Stretch: Why do trained athletes recover faster?
independent.a: Stronger heart and lungs deliver oxygen faster, so less lactic acid builds and the debt is repaid sooner.

exit.q: Anaerobic means...
exit.a: Without oxygen

exit.q: Big question: why keep panting after a sprint?
exit.a: To repay the oxygen debt by breaking down lactic acid.

lessons.homework: Explain oxygen debt to someone at home, using your graph.
lessons.send: SEND: table pre-drawn. EAL: anaerobic, lactic acid. Stretch: research why marathon runners pace themselves.

lessons.title: Fermentation: yeast, sugar and a balloon
lessons.bigQuestion: Bread dough doubles in size in a warm kitchen but hardly rises in the fridge. What is the yeast doing differently?
objectives: To understand how yeast respires anaerobically and how temperature affects the rate
successCriteria: All: write the word equation for fermentation
Most: set up the yeast and balloon practical
Some: explain the effect of temperature using the results
lessons.crossCurricular: DT: the science of bread making
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: bread as a blessing

keywords.def: a single-celled fungus
anaerobic respiration in yeast
a type of alcohol made by fermentation
the gas that makes bread rise
a protein that speeds up reactions in cells

hook.text: Bread dough doubles in size in a warm kitchen but hardly rises in the fridge. What is the yeast doing differently?
hook.a: Yeast respires faster when warm, making more carbon dioxide; cold slows its enzymes.

islamicLink.text: Fermentation is how bread rises, a blessing we eat every day. It also makes alcohol, which Allah has forbidden: 'intoxicants ... are defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it' (Al-Ma'idah 5:90). In bread the small amount of ethanol is driven off in the oven.

teach.heading: Fermentation
teach.note: In bread the ethanol evaporates in the oven.

teach.heading: Safety guide: yeast balloon
bullets: Warm water from the tap (like a warm bath), never from the kettle
An adult helps stretch the balloon
Do not drink or taste the mixture; wash hands after
Do not seal bottles with a lid
teach.note: Read the written guide aloud together; pupils tick each rule on the portal sheet before they start.

teach.heading: Method
bullets: Three bottles: cold, warm, hot tap water
Same yeast (1 sachet), sugar (2 tsp), water (100 ml)
Balloon on each; measure circumference every 10 min

check.q: Why did the hot bottle make little gas?
options: Yeast enzymes were damaged by heat
check.why: High temperatures denature enzymes and kill yeast.

practice.q: Write the word equation for fermentation.
practice.model: Reactant: glucose. Anaerobic in yeast gives two products: ethanol and carbon dioxide.

practice.q: What is the variable you change?
Name two variables you keep the same.

independent.q: Core: Set up the three bottles with an adult, measure the balloons every 10 minutes for 30 minutes, record and draw a bar chart.
independent.a: Pupils' own; warm bottle inflates most
independent.model: Teacher sets up the warm bottle on camera and measures 15 cm at the start.

independent.q: Extend: Explain the results using enzymes.
independent.a: Warm temperatures speed up enzymes so more CO₂ is made; cold slows them; hot denatures them.

independent.q: Stretch: Why do bakers knead dough in a warm room but bake it in a very hot oven?
independent.a: Warm room: yeast makes CO₂ so dough rises; hot oven kills yeast, sets the bread and evaporates the ethanol.

exit.q: Fermentation makes ethanol and...
exit.a: Carbon dioxide

exit.q: Big question: why does dough rise in a warm kitchen but not the fridge?
exit.a: Yeast respires faster when warm, making more carbon dioxide.

lessons.homework: Help an adult bake simple bread and watch the dough rise. Write what the yeast was doing.
lessons.send: SEND: table pre-drawn. EAL: yeast, ferment, gas. Stretch: test the effect of sugar amount instead.

without oxygen

hook.text: Respiration is happening in every one of your cells right now. Which fact from this unit amazes you most?

practice.q: What is oxygen debt?

practice.q: Why does warm dough rise faster?
